newsitem.title: USA: SEC adopts new anti-manipulative rule on offerings.
newsitem.headline: SEC adopts new anti-manipulative rule on offerings.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday adopted new rules designed to prevent manipulation of securities offerings.
The new rules at the same time ease restrictions that currently hamper activities of issuers, underwriters and other participants during an offering period.

The commission, which has been heavily critized for taking too long to review merger applications in a rapidly changing market, said it would aim to issue decisions within 12 to 15 months of receiving a completed merger application.
Commissioners, who approved the new guidelines unanimously, said the main goal of their policy statement was to make sure that new merged utilities did not thwart a competitive market.
"We do not want to see mergers that are counter to that goal," FERC Chairwoman Elizabeth Moler said.

Updating a 30-year-old policy for reviewing mergers, the commission said it would no longer try to measure the cost and benefits of a merger. Nine utility mergers worth about $25 billion are now pending before the commission.

Under the new regulation, transactions by distribution participants in securities with an average trading volume of $1 million or more and whose issuers have a public float of at least $150 million would not be restricted.
This would eliminate retrictions on equity securities of approximately 1,900 domestic issuers and many foreign issuers, said Richard Lindsey, SEC's market regulation chief.
The period of trading restrictions for most securities would be reduced to one or five business days, from the current two or nine business days, depending on the type of security.

Trading restrictions on derivatives during an offering of the associated security would be eliminated. Trading restrictions owuld be imposed on the associated security would be imposed, however, when its derivative security is distributed.
Transactions in most debt, preferred and asset-backed securities would be deregulations.
In all, Regulation M encompasses six new rules that governs the activities of underwrtiers, brokers, dealers, other distribution participants and others involved in securities offerings.
